e-12428.problem:
Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = u - v - 2, \qquad y = v - u + 5.
$$

Suppose that $A$ is the matrix representing the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/b3d58dc3ce18b0f5c977b930088152bb7b9c4c821edb656bc478904b67ae8acf.png)

- $\det(A) = 0$

- The transformation is invertible
e-12428.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-2 \\ v-u+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ -u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/83207d393e930561d8d1f45fb0b21a61f0af7350bfc684f38e846a2cebd1493b.png)

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/01afe0c9e10a71665dc2ea7d4bd076bb2b9ba63e8dff10d6fbd3264a88008c39.png)

- Statement III is false. Since $\det(A) = 0,$ the affine transformation is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

e-12429.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Matrix Form
e-12429.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/6cce99dca6804d7a15dbf107312e367d45c2e9ef917e7f212fba56a018b6ae5f.png)

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/3b195dda0cddb83bb414ff40ec076286765b7f599e1bac8cc7d04bdd6e9273e2.png)
e-12429.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $\mathbf T$ gives us the following information:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/ead1edec5d6fa82de8eb0137a838826221e0f45093782bc1b0a32111b05a37f4.png)

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot 7-(-9)\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = -7 + 3 + 8 = 4.
$$

e-12430.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Parametric Form
e-12430.problem:
The affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is defined as

$$
x = u - v + 2, \qquad y = 4u - 5v + 9.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ of $\mathbf T$ is

$$
u = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{a}x - y + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{b}, \qquad v = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{c}x - y + 1,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
e-12430.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $\mathbf{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+2 \\ 4u-5v+9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ 4u-5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-5)-(-1)\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y-9) \\ 4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y-9)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5x-y-1 \\ 4x-y+1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{5}x - y + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{(-1)}, \qquad v = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{4}x - y + 1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c = 5 + (-1) + 4 = 8.
$$

e-12441.knowledge_point: Identifying the Types of Images Formed by an Affine Transformation
e-12441.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/8797a50ddc0750a97190f96d8bc1cffe70c6ef9cc8e55a46f5a75d6b6702c81d.png)

Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T,$ given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/347a44c388bd81e78d4dcf5f40584ce76273ffe25513ebb1522568ba479ac4fc.png) 
Describe the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}.$
e-12441.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{u} \longrightarrow A \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{b},
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., when $\det(A) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., when $\det(A) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf{T}$ is 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097781/assets/94625329d7eba1da88a9dde36b6e64335a9801658a8c1fd054cea9db835ea4fa.png)

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 2-4\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $\mathbf{T}$ is non-invertible and the image of the triangle under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is a line segment.

Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

  1. T1:[uv]⟶[−2u−5v−94u+9v−9]
  2. T2:[uv]⟶[3u+3v+43u+3v−1]
  3. T3:[uv]⟶[3u+v8]

decision.explanation: An affine transformation is invertible exactly when its linear coefficient matrix has nonzero determinant. For T₁, the determinant is (-2)(9)-(-5)(4)=2. For T₂, it is 3·3-3·3=0. For T₃, the second row is zero, so its determinant is 0. Thus only T₁ is invertible.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 8\end{aligned}]$
after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v \\ 4u+9v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}|=9\cdot (-2)-(-5)\cdot 4=2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+3v \\ 3u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 3-3\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=0\cdot 3-1\cdot 0=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ only."

Question 1
?

Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

  1. T1:[uv]⟶[−2u−5v−94u+9v−9]
  2. T2:[uv]⟶[3u+3v+43u+3v−1]
  3. T3:[uv]⟶[3u+v8]
a
T1 and T3 only
b
T2 only
c
T3 only
d
T1 and T2 only
e
T1 only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

An affine transformation T:R2→R2 is a function of the form x=Au+b, where x,u, and b are column vectors in R2, and A is a 2×2 matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix A is invertible. That is, if det(A)≠0.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation T1 is invertible. Notice that T1 can be expressed as [xy]=[−2u−5v−94u+9v−9]=[−2u−5v4u+9v]+[−9−9]=[−2−549]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[−9−9]⏟b. Computing the determinant of A, we get det(A)=|−2−549|=9⋅(−2)−(−5)⋅4=2≠0. Since the determinant is nonzero, T1 is invertible.

  • Transformation T2 is not invertible. Notice that T2 can be expressed as [xy]=[3u+3v+43u+3v−1]=[3u+3v3u+3v]+[4−1]=[3333]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[4−1]⏟b. Computing the determinant of A, we get det(A)=|3333|=3⋅3−3⋅3=0. Since the determinant is zero, T2 is not invertible.

  • Transformation T3 is not invertible. Notice that T3 can be expressed as [xy]=[3u+v8]=[3u+v0]+[08]=[3100]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[08]⏟b. Computing the determinant of A, we get det(A)=|3100|=0⋅3−1⋅0=0. Since the determinant is zero, T3 is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "T1 only."

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations
content.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 8\end{aligned}]$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v-9 \\ 4u+9v-9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2u-5v \\ 4u+9v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ -9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 4 & 9\end{aligned}|=9\cdot (-2)-(-5)\cdot 4=2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+3v+4 \\ 3u+3v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+3v \\ 3u+3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 3-3\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=0\cdot 3-1\cdot 0=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ only."

Question 2
?

Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

  1. T1:[uv]⟶[5u−2v−510u−4v+1]
  2. T2:[uv]⟶[u−v−4u+5v+7]
  3. T3:[uv]⟶[2u+4v−23u+6v+3]
a
T2 and T3 only
b
T1 only
c
T2 only
d
T1 and T3 only
e
T1 and T2 only
Submit

decision.explanation: An affine transformation is invertible exactly when its linear matrix has nonzero determinant. For T₁: 5(-4)-(-2)(10)=0. For T₂: 1(5)-(-1)(1)=6. For T₃: 2(6)-4(3)=0. Therefore, only T₂ is invertible.

after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{aligned}|=-4\cdot 5-(-2)\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-4 \\ u+5v+7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

  1. T1:[uv]⟶[5u−2v−510u−4v+1]
  2. T2:[uv]⟶[u−v−4u+5v+7]
  3. T3:[uv]⟶[2u+4v−23u+6v+3]
a
T2 and T3 only
b
T1 only
c
T2 only
d
T1 and T3 only
e
T1 and T2 only
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

An affine transformation T:R2→R2 is a function of the form x=Au+b, where x,u, and b are column vectors in R2, and A is a 2×2 matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix A is invertible. That is, if det(A)≠0.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation T1 is not invertible. Notice that T1 can be expressed as [xy]=[5u−2v−510u−4v+1]=[5u−2v10u−4v]+[−51]=[5−210−4]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[−51]⏟b. Computing the determinant of A, we get det(A)=|5−210−4|=−4⋅5−(−2)⋅10=0. Since the determinant is zero, T1 is not invertible.

  • Transformation T2 is invertible. Notice that T2 can be expressed as [xy]=[u−v−4u+5v+7]=[u−vu+5v]+[−47]=[1−115]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[−47]⏟b. Computing the determinant of A, we get det(A)=|1−115|=5⋅1−(−1)⋅1=6≠0. Since the determinant is nonzero, T2 is invertible.

  • Transformation T3 is not invertible. Notice that T3 can be expressed as [xy]=[2u+4v−23u+6v+3]=[2u+4v3u+6v]+[−23]=[2436]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[−23]⏟b. Computing the determinant of A, we get det(A)=|2436|=6⋅2−4⋅3=0. Since the determinant is zero, T3 is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "T2 only."

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations
content.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}5u-2v-5 \\ 10u-4v+1\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u-v-4 \\ u+5v+7\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2u+4v-2 \\ 3u+6v+3\end{aligned}]$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5u-2v-5 \\ 10u-4v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5u-2v \\ 10u-4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ 10 & -4\end{aligned}|=-4\cdot 5-(-2)\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v-4 \\ u+5v+7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}|=5\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 1=6\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u+4v-2 \\ 3u+6v+3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u+4v \\ 3u+6v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}|=6\cdot 2-4\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{2}$ only."

decision.explanation: An affine transformation is invertible when its linear matrix has nonzero determinant. For T₁, det=1·7−1·(−2)=9. For T₂, det=2·2−1·4=0. For T₃, det=1·7−0·8=7. Therefore, T₁ and T₃ only are invertible.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{aligned}]$
after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+v+6 \\ 7v-2u+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+v \\ -2u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot 1-1\cdot (-2)=9\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u+v-2 \\ 4+4u+2v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u+v \\ 4u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u+9 \\ 8u+7v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u \\ 8u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot 1-0\cdot 8=7.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{3}$ only."

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{aligned}]$
after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6u+3v \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}|=5\cdot 6-3\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=4\cdot (-3)-(-4)\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot (-6)-(-4)\cdot 8=-10\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{3}$ only."

\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6u+3v+3 \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6u+3v \\ 10u+5v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}|=5\cdot 6-3\cdot 10=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{1}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v-2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3u-4v \\ 3u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-3 & -4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=4\cdot (-3)-(-4)\cdot 3=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{2}$ is *not* invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v-7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6u-4v \\ 8u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 8 & 7\end{aligned}|=7\cdot (-6)-(-4)\cdot 8=-10\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{3}$ is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{3}$ only."

decision.explanation: An affine transformation is invertible exactly when its linear matrix has nonzero determinant. For T₁: (−1)(1)−(1)(1)=−2. For T₂: (1)(−1)−(0)(1)=−1. For T₃: (3)(2)−(6)(1)=0. Therefore, T₁ and T₂ only are invertible.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Which of the following affine transformations are invertible?

- ${T}_{1}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}v-u \\ u+v\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{2}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}]$
- ${T}_{3}:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3u+6v \\ u+2v-1\end{aligned}]$
after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

The transformation is invertible if the matrix $A$ is invertible. That is, if $det(A)\ne 0.$

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

- Transformation ${T}_{1}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{1}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-u \\ u+v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=(-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 1=-2\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{1}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{2}$ is invertible. Notice that ${T}_{2}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u \\ u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|=1\cdot (-1)-0\cdot 1=-1\ne 0.
$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+6v \\ u+2v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+6v \\ u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 2-6\cdot 1=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only."

\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-2 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u \\ u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$

$$

Since the determinant is nonzero, ${T}_{2}$ is invertible.

- Transformation ${T}_{3}$ is not invertible. Notice that ${T}_{3}$ can be expressed as

$$

$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 2-6\cdot 1=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, ${T}_{3}$ is *not* invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$ only."

$$

$$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 2-1\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

The matrix form of the affine transformation T is given by

[xy]=[−324−2]⋅[uv]+[−47].

Find a+b+c, given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation T−1 is given by

[uv]=[11ab][xy]+[−3c].

a
−3
b
0
c
1

−1
e
4

decision.explanation: The determinant is −2, giving inverse matrix [[1,1],[2,3/2]]. The inverse translation is −[[1,1],[2,3/2]][−4,7]ᵀ=[−3,−5/2]ᵀ. Thus a+b+c=2+3/2−5/2=1.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ a & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-2\cdot (-3)-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+\frac{3}{2}+(-\frac{5}{2})=1.
$$

The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ a & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-2\cdot (-3)-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+\frac{3}{2}+(-\frac{5}{2})=1.
$$

Question 8
?

The matrix form of the affine transformation T is given by

[xy]=[1259]⋅[uv]+[24].

Find a+b+c, given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation T−1 is given by

[uv]=[a2b−1][xy]+[10c].

a
5
b
4
c
−7
d
−2
e
−10
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

An affine transformation T:R2→R2 is a function of the form x=Au+b, where x,u, and b are column vectors in R2, and A is a 2×2 matrix.

Reversing the action of T, we get

Au+b=xAu=x−bu=A−1(x−b).

The matrix form of T gives us the following information:

[1259]⏟A⋅[uv]⏟u+[24]⏟b

Next, we calculate the inverse of A:

A−1=19⋅1−2⋅5[9−2−51]=1−1[9−2−51]=[−925−1]

Therefore, the inverse transformation T−1 is

[uv]⏟u=[−925−1]⏟A−1⋅([xy]⏟x−[24]⏟b)=[−925−1][xy]−[−925−1][24]=[−925−1][xy]−[−106]=[−925−1][xy]+[10−6].

Therefore, we have a+b+c=−9+5+(−6)=−10.

content.knowledge_point: Inverting Affine Transformations Given in Matrix Form
content.problem:
The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Find $a+b+c,$ given that the matrix form of the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}a & 2 \\ b & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}10 \\ c\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix form of $T$ gives us the following information:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 9\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 1-2\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 2 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}-9 & 2 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 2 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-9 & 2 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 2 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 2 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-9+5+(-6)=-10.
$$

content.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=5u-9v-2,\,y=4u-8v+4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-\frac{9}{4}y+b,\,v=cx-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5u-9v-2 \\ 4u-8v+4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5u-9v \\ 4u-8v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}5 & -9 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-8\cdot 5-(-9)\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-4}[\begin{aligned}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ y-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+2)-\frac{9}{4}\cdot (y-4) \\ 1\cdot (x+2)+(-\frac{5}{4})\cdot (y-4)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13 \\ x-\frac{5}{4}y+7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13,\,v=1x-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+13+1=16.
$$

$$
x=Au+b,

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v-4 \\ 2u-4v-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-3v \\ 2u-4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

after.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=5v-7u+3,\,y=7v-10u+5.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-5y+4,\,v=bx+cy+5,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
after.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5v-7u+3 \\ 7v-10u+5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7u+5v \\ -10u+7v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-7 & 5 \\ -10 & 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{7\cdot (-7)-5\cdot (-10)}[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -5 \\ 10 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-3 \\ y-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7\cdot (x-3)+(-5)\cdot (y-5) \\ 10\cdot (x-3)+(-7)\cdot (y-5)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7x-5y+4 \\ 10x-7y+5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7x-5y+4,\,v=10x+(-7)y+5.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=7+10+(-7)=10.
$$

content.problem:
The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=-2v-4,\,y=u+4v+6.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=bx+cy-2,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
content.worked_solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2v-4 \\ u+4v+6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2v \\ u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x+4 \\ y-6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\cdot (x+4)+1\cdot (y-6) \\ (-\frac{1}{2})\cdot (x+4)+0\cdot (y-6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2x+y+2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}x-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+2,\,v=(-\frac{1}{2})x+0y-2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2+(-\frac{1}{2})+0=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot 6 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible, and the image of the pentagon under the action of $T$ is a line segment.

content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ 4u-v+2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ 4u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot (-1)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}

after.worked_solution:
Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-2v+1 \\ 2u-3v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-2v \\ 2u-3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}].$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-3)-2\cdot (-2) \\  & =1 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a non-singular matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is invertible and the image of the triangle under the action of $T$ is a triangle.
